summary: Defines a management information base (MIB) for SNMP so that Mobile IP mobile nodes, foreign agents, and home agents can be monitored and managed. It lists the objects that network tools can read.

eli5.summary: It is a menu of dials and gauges that lets a manager check on the machines that help devices roam.

subtitle: The SNMP dials and gauges for watching Mobile IP mobile nodes, foreign agents and home agents.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP lets a host keep its IP address while it moves between networks, but operators had no standard way to configure or monitor the mobile node, foreign agent and home agent with SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the MIP-MIB, a set of SNMP objects split into groups per Mobile IP entity, covering system settings, security associations, agent discovery, registrations and mobility bindings.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read counters and tables from each Mobile IP entity and trigger a notification on authentication failures. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Entities managed
facts.value: Mobile Node, Foreign Agent, Home Agent

today: RFC 2006 is a Proposed Standard published in October 1996. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It manages the protocol described in RFC 2002.

sections.title: The SNMP Framework Behind the MIB
sections.content:
RFC 2006 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing the Mobile IP protocol. The abstract says it describes managed objects for the Mobile Node, the Foreign Agent and the Home Agent.

It sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which the RFC lists as three parts: the SMI (RFC 1902) for describing and naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of objects, and the protocol itself (RFC 1157 and/or RFC 1905) for accessing them.

Each object is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the object type plus an instance identifies one specific value. The module itself is placed at mib-2 44.
sections.eli5: A MIB is like a numbered catalog of every gauge on a machine. Each gauge has its own catalog number, so a manager can ask for exactly the one it wants.

sections.title: The Three Mobile IP Entities
sections.content:
The MIB follows the model of Mobile IP, which introduces three functional entities.

  • A Mobile Node is a host or router that changes its point of attachment from one network to another without changing its IP address.
  • A Home Agent is a router on the mobile node's home network. It tunnels packets to the mobile node when it is away and keeps its current location.
  • A Foreign Agent is a router on the visited network. It provides routing services to the registered mobile node, detunnels packets the home agent sent, and may act as default router for datagrams the mobile node sends.

The document specifies the objects used to manage exactly these three entities.
sections.eli5: Think of a traveler with a permanent home mailbox. The home post office forwards the mail, and the hotel front desk hands it over. The traveler is the mobile node, the home post office is the home agent, and the hotel desk is the foreign agent.

sections.title: How Objects Were Chosen
sections.content:
The authors applied four selection criteria, which they say follow IAB directives and good engineering practice.

  1. Split management functions among the mobile node, home agent and foreign agent the same way the Mobile IP protocol splits them.
  2. Require that objects be essential for fault or configuration management.
  3. Limit the total number of objects.
  4. Leave out objects that can simply be derived from others in this or other MIBs.
sections.eli5: The authors only put in the gauges that really help you fix or set up the machine. They left out gauges that just repeat what other gauges already say.

sections.title: MIB Groups and Who Implements Them
sections.content:
Objects are arranged into groups, and each group applies to one or more entities. Three groups apply to all of them: mipSystemGroup, mipSecAssociationGroup and mipSecViolationGroup.

The mobile node adds mnSystemGroup, mnDiscoveryGroup and mnRegistrationGroup. Both the foreign agent and the home agent implement maAdvertisementGroup for agent advertisements. The foreign agent also has faSystemGroup, faAdvertisementGroup and faRegistrationGroup. The home agent has haRegistrationGroup and haRegNodeCountersGroup.
sections.eli5: Some gauges are on every helper machine, and some only belong to one kind of helper. The memo has a chart showing which is which.

sections.title: What Each Entity Exposes
sections.content:
Everything is defined in the MIP-MIB module. Under mipSystem, mipEntities says which entities a device supports (mobile node, foreign agent, home agent, possibly several), mipEnable turns Mobile IP on or off, and mipEncapsulationSupported lists the supported encapsulation methods: ipInIp, gre, minEnc or other.

The mobile node reports mnState (home, registered, pending, isolated or unknown), its mnHomeAddress, tables of potential home agents and foreign agents, discovery counters such as mnSolicitationsSent and mnAdvertisementsReceived, and a registration table with counters for requests sent and replies received.

The foreign agent has a table of supported care-of addresses, flags faIsBusy and faRegistrationRequired that map to the 'B' and 'R' bits in its advertisements, a visitor table, and counters for requests relayed and the reasons for refusing them.

The home agent keeps a mobility binding table, indexed by mobile node and care-of address, and per-node counters including the most recent denial code (haRecentServiceDeniedCode), plus totals such as haProxyARPsSent. Registration flags are a BITS textual convention with six bits.
sections.eli5: The mobile node can tell you where it is and whether it has checked in. The hotel desk can tell you who is staying and whether it is too busy. The home post office keeps a list of where each traveler's mail is going.

sections.title: Security Associations and Violations
sections.content:
The mipSecAssocTable holds Mobility Security Associations, indexed by the peer's IP address and a 4-byte SPI. Each row records the algorithm type (other or md5), the mode (other or prefixSuffix), a shared key of 16 octets, and the replay-protection method (other, timestamps or nonces). Reading the key always returns a zero-length value.

A separate violations table counts problems per violator, with the most recent SPI, time, identification and a reason such as badAuthenticator, badIdentifier, badSPI or missingSecurityExtension. The optional mipAuthFailure notification reports an authentication failure when the entity validates a registration request or reply.
sections.eli5: Each pair of machines shares a secret handshake. The memo lets you set the handshake but never read it back, and it keeps a log of everyone who got the handshake wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the MIB lets an operator configure Mobile IP authentication and the shared secret key, which is a security risk. It lists four mitigations.

  • Risky variables sit in separate groups, so an implementor may choose not to implement them.
  • The agent always returns a zero-length string when the key is read, so it cannot leak through SNMP GET, GET-NEXT or GET-BULK.
  • A trap tells the manager about security violations.
  • A violation table logs them for later analysis.

An implementation SHOULD allow access to this MIB only via SNMPv2 with other security enhancements such as SNMPv2Sec, or together with the IP Authentication Header and IP Encapsulating Security Payload.
sections.eli5: Some of the switches are dangerous, so they are kept in their own box that makers can leave out. The secret key can be set but never read back.
